articles.text: As I write it is Maundy Thursday 2023. Tonight, many Christians will hold communion services recalling Jesus’ last supper with his disciples. Some of the services will include ceremonial foot washings recognizing that Jesus, modeling servanthood, washed the feet of his disciples. Tomorrow, there will be Good Friday services aplenty. Some of them will last three hours and include sermons on the “Seven Last Words” of Jesus, a compilation of the seven sayings the four gospels record Jesus speaking from the cross. Woven into almost all the services will be the refrain “Jesus died for our sins.” Accompanying these words will be the very widespread interpretation of the crucifixion as some sort of atoning sacrifice, of Jesus laying down his life to make payment for our sins. Almost reluctantly – for to question the theology of substitutionary atonement is heretical to many – I find it necessary to note that this is not the only possible way to interpret the crucifixion. Indeed, from very early times there has been, and continues to be, lively debate about how best to interpret and how best to understand the death of Jesus. articles.text: Dr. James Allison (front, left) with California Colorectal Cancer Coalition board members. Last February, longtime Piedmont resident Dr. James Allison received a 2023 Visionary Award from the California Colorectal Cancer Coalition (C4) for championing low-cost colorectal cancer screening options. The award is among many lifetime achievements for Allison. He is also a C4 Board Member; a retired gastroenterologist from Kaiser Oakland Medical Center; a Fellow of the American College of Physicians and of the American Gastroenterological Association; a Clinical Professor of Medicine Emeritus at UCSF; and a member of the Division of Gastroenterology at UCSF and the San Francisco General Hospital. Other notable professional awards he has received include the Lowell Beal, MD Award from Kaiser Oakland Medical Center “in appreciation of his example of academic excellence combined with warm humanity” (1996); the Premier Physician Award from the Bay Area Chapter of the Crohn’s and Colitis Foundation (2003); and the Distinguished Clinician Award from the American Gastroenterological Association (2004). Since 2000, Dr. Allison has worked as an ad hoc consultant to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), the National Cancer Institute (NCI), and the Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality (AHRQ) on issues concerned with screening for colorectal cancer. Over the course of his career Allison has become a national and international expert on colorectal cancer screening. He was the first person in the U.S. to show, in a publication in The New England Journal of Medicine in 1996, that a certain kind of fecal immunochemical test (FIT) was superior to the standard guaiac fecal occult blood test being used for screening for colorectal cancer. Speaking on the FIT test, he said, “Many countries in the rest of the world have been using stool tests for years; the U.S. is an outlier. Until around 2012, all that people were told they could have for colon cancer prevention was a colonoscopy. It’s very important to test for colon cancer, but you don’t have to spend that money or go through that hassle” as opposed to a FIT test. Currently, Allison works with C4 and the California and San Francisco Departments of Public Health to increase colorectal cancer screening rates in underserved populations by instituting a FIT-based screening program in clinics served by safety net hospitals. Dr. Allison’s screening and IBD research has been published in the Annals of Internal Medicine, The New England Journal of Medicine, Gastroenterology, Clinical Gastroenterology and Hepatology, the Journal of the National Cancer Institute and other peer-reviewed journals. He has been quoted in Prevention Magazine, the Ladies’ Home Journal, the Wall Street Journal, the San Francisco Chronicle and the New York Times.

articles.text: Piedmont City Council approved a new traffic and safety design plan at Nova Drive and Magnolia Avenue at its meeting on April 3. The current painted-stripe “bollard island”, approved by Council in April 2019 and installed that year in July, will be replaced by a permanent, curb-defined traffic island with a pedestrian crosswalk through it. The island will provide direction to westbound drivers on Magnolia. The plan also includes an eastbound left turn pocket to allow sight distance for vehicles turning left from Magnolia onto Nova. The traffic island will be treated with mulch to allow for easy landscaping, and will be shaped to allow driveway access for all neighboring residents. A bulb-out will also be added to the 101 corner of Magnolia for traffic making the turn downhill and right onto Nova. The plan will not restrict or eliminate any currently available street parking. The total estimated construction cost is $100,000. Bids will open in late spring and construction is expected to begin soon afterward this summer. At the meeting, Public Works Director Daniel Gonzales said that the project “goes back at least 10 years,” and was included in the Pedestrian and Bicycle Master Plan adopted in 2015. However, the bollards have been met with constructive criticism from neighbors who contend that bollard configuration is both unsightly and confusing to drivers, doing little to protect pedestrians. In May 2022, 120 residents signed a petition asking the city to make permanent improvements to the 3-way intersection. The “bollard island” at Nova Drive and Magnolia Avenue is expected to be replaced this summer by a permanent traffic island. The city temporarily closed the area in December 2022 due to hazardous conditions created by the first in a series of heavy rains. Slippery conditions, soil erosion, and unstable walking surfaces were exacerbated during the weeks of severe storms in January 2023, forcing an extended closure. The dog area re-opened briefly on February 20, only to close again due to rain four days later. For the last several weeks, the Public Works staff has regularly inspected the site to determine how and when the dog area could re-open. articles.text: The Salvation Army will hold its eighth annual gala on Sunday, April 30 at 5 p.m. at the University Club in UC Berkeley’s Memorial Stadium. Chaired by Debbie Kelley of Piedmont, the event will feature live music from the UC Berkeley a cappella group DeCadence, live and silent auctions, testimonials from inspiring Salvation Army beneficiaries, and dinner. The Volunteer of the Year honoree Elijah Hicks, will be introduced. A former UC Berkeley football player, he was drafted by the Chicago Bears last year and has chosen the Salvation Army for philanthropy through his foundation, Intercept Poverty. The organization provides financial assistance to low-income students. All proceeds will help fund The Salvation Army’s efforts to meet human need in Alameda County. The non-profit helps with food, rent, and utility assistance, operates a homeless shelter and homeless outreach programs, preschools, after-school programs, a summer camp in the Sierra foothills, music programs, Christmas assistance, and workforce development programs in construction and certified nurse’s assistant training. Kelley, who is chairing the event for her fourth year, has been on the Salvation Army advisory board since 2016. She confirmed that last year’s gala raised over $420,000 with 150 people in attendance. A similar crowd is expected this year. “The people involved before me said they were lucky to clear $100,000,” said Kelley. “Now we clear $300,000-$400,000, much due Corki Recht, the co-chair for three years.” When Kelley was unavailable last year due to an emergency, Recht ran the event, the first time the gala was held at Memorial Stadium, In prior years it had been held at the Claremont Country Club. Wanting a change of venue, Kelley, who works in ColEvent co-chairs Corki Recht and Debbie Kelley. lege Relations at UC Berkeley, approached the school’s Athletics Director, Jim Knowlton, who encouraged the move. “It was then that we decided to honor a Cal student volunteer,” said Kelley. In 2022 the honoree was professional baseball player Tyson Ross, a pitcher who has created a “Loyal to my Soil” program providing baseball lessons to inner-city children. Highlights at this year’s live auction includes a dinner for 10 cooked by Salvation Army Culinary Director Tim Tucker, and a testimonial by Thomas Wolf, a former homeless man and drug addict who has since reinvented his life due to his work with the Salvation Army. “People think of the Salvation Army as red kettles and thrift stores,” said Kelley, “but they provide such important rehabilitation and emergency service work. They help and employ people in need, and do not discriminate as to who they help. The gala is a wonderful opportunity for Piedmonters to celebrate this spirit of charity.” Individual tickets start at $250. articles.text: Piedmont’s community reading project, Readmont, now in its 13th year, has selected No Stopping Us Now by Lucy Jane Bledsoe as this year’s collective read. It was chosen to help celebrate the 50th anniversary of Title IX, the federal legislation requiring equal funding for women’s and men’s sports. It is a book about the love of sports, finding one’s own voice, and activism. Led by Piedmont High School English Department Chair Beth Black, Readmont will host a community discussion with the author on Wednesday, April 26, at 7:00 p.m. in the Piedmont High School library. Based on the author’s true story, it is a compelling examination of standing up for what is right. The book follows the story of Louisa who fought to bring her hometown into compliance with the new Title IX law so she could play basketball at her high school in Oregon. Those interested in discussing the book and learning more about the author are encouraged to attend the evening event. English department chairperson Black will also lead discussions during lunchtime on April 25 and 26. Books are available for check out at all Piedmont school libraries. Books are funded through the support of the Title IX celebration committee and the Piedmont No Stopping Us Now by Lucy Jane Bledsoe was named a Finalist for both the Golden Poppy Award and the Rainbow Award. articles.text: Piedmont and Millennium High School students gathered in the Alan Harvey theater and Binks Rawlings gym on Friday, April 7, for a Diversity Assembly, “I am Here,” in which students presented stories of facing microaggressions, misinformation, and bullying. Organized by PHS junior Valentina Prieto Black, with the help of PHS Theater teacher Kimberly Taylor, the assembly amplified the voices of students with diverse experiences and perspectives. The gathering highlighted Black, Asian, Latinx, gay and transgender identities, and hardships including struggles with racism, eating disorders, and depression. Students presented their own stories and the stories of classmates who submitted their stories anonymously. The assembly came at the end of ‘Diversity Week,’ during which different affinity clubs and student unions were given a platform at lunchtime to educate students about the various backgrounds, cultures, and histories that make up the student body. Prieto Black is the president elect of the school’s “Diversity Committee,” a club that began in 2017 that unites many affinity groups and student leaders. The club has hosted diversity assemblies in 2018 and 2019 and continued its work during the COVID pandemic. articles.text: On Thursday, April 6, the Piedmont Community Church parking lot was filled with eager teens, parents, and adult volunteers loading vans and trucks with supplies and packed bags ahead of the church’s annual Spring Break trip. More than 200 students in the church youth group left for Mexico Sunday morning, April 9, for five days outside Tijuana, Mexico, where they will build 12 houses for impoverished Mexican families. The church’s annual Treasures Sale last month raised $27,000 toward the cost of building materials, food, and travel costs. For more than 24 years, the church has sent volunteers south of the border to build homes for families who often have never had a real roof or a front door that locks. For the community of Piedmont, the Mexico trip has become a rite of passage for Piedmont teens, and often their first direct contact with poverty. When Scott Kail, the church youth minister and leader of the Mission Trip, first went to Mexico in 2004, the crew consisted of 25 to 30 students and adults in total. They built two homes. This week they will build 15 homes. Kail explained that over the years attendance has grown to its “current count of 220 students, 15 teams and 35 adult leaders — two adults for each team — plus 15 adult kitchen crew members, probably the hardest worker of all. Kitchen crews commonly have 12-hour days.” Each of the 15 teams will have its own van. The teams are color coded, and each member wears a distinctive t-shirt with the team color (Peach, Orange, Maroon, Navy). The volunteers will work Monday through Thursday, April 10-13. The houses are 11-feet by 22-feet, each with two rooms, two windows, and a locking front door. Each crew begins by hand-mixing concrete to pour for the foundation slab. On following days they build and erect the house frames, and cover the roofs with tar paper. bailing wire, tar paper, and chicken wire so the homes can be completed with stucco on the fourth day. For Yellow Team Leader Garrett Kail, son of Scott, this will be his ninth Mexico trip. His first four years were as a high school student. “Hands down, this is my favorite week of the year,” Garrett said. “The trip’s impact is almost unexplainable if you don’t experience it yourself. The combination of kindness, fun, hard work, and compassion is at an intensity that I think is nearly impossible to find in everyday life.” “I do it for the love of it, and to serve,” he added. “I’ve seen how the Mission Trip has grown since my father took over the leadership, and he’s always been doing his best work with it. It’s so obvious that this is where his heart is.” Feeding an army of over 200 volunteers is a task on its own. The mess hall tent is constantly in use, with dedicated cooks prepping, cooking, and serving food from morning to evening. articles.text: Recently, my eleven-year-old decided to start journaling. He had never journaled before, but he was chatting with me about all the thoughts that he had in his head and how they sometimes can get stuck. I suggested that he could write them all down and that might feel good. I have not been a regular journal-er for a while, but in the interest of supporting him, I told him that I would journal as well. So, a few weeks ago, I picked him up from school and went to find the right journal. Since then, we have both been journaling daily. He has chosen to do five minutes before bed and five minutes when he first wakes up and I am writing before bed every night for about 10 minutes. When I think about living a creative life, one of the challenges that I find and that I hear from others is the concept of time pressure. I don’t have time to add more things into my day, but I wonder how much of that time scarcity is less about actual time and is more about Creative Capacity. After all, most of us find time to scroll Instagram or watch the latest episode of “Love is Blind”. our ability to have new ideas, identify original thoughts, come up with novel activities. That time scarcity might be our way of protecting ourselves because our Creative Capacity is low, so we are scared that it will just tax our minds too much to have to come up with one more new idea. And that’s where journaling has really drawn my attention, The more that I have journaled daily, the easier it is to put pen to paper and write. The first few nights I had that hurdle of the “blank page” to overcome. I thought it mattered what I wrote down and I stressed myself out trying to make it “meaningful.” It took cognitive power to come up with an idea or search my brain for what wanted to come out. The more I did it, the easier that barrier to entry became. The words flowed more smoothly. The ideas were just there; I didn’t have to search to find them. My Creat ive Capacit y increased because of Creative Consistency. Creative Consistency means that we embark on a creative process with regularity. The same way that when we go to the gym three days a week, lifting weights feels achievable. When we only go sporadically, every time feels hard. If we choose to do something small every day with our creative superpowers – a mini painting, a doodle board, singing along to one song, dancing for three minutes, doing a journal before bed – that Creative Consistency gives us the lubrication to increase our Creative Capacity because our minds and bodies are primed and ready to go! articles.text: Nearly 100 members and friends of Piedmont Community Church celebrated Associate Pastor Don Ashburn’s 20 years of outstanding service to the congregation at a ceremony on Sunday, April 2, With the cooperation of the weather (finally), people gathered in the church Courtyard after worship for cake and heartfelt recollections about how much Don has meant to so many. Don’s wife, Margaret Ovenden, and his two adult children, Griffin and Madeline, were present for the milestone event. Immediate Past President of the Board of Trustees Jan Wolfe emphasized Don’s pastoral skills, which she experienced profoundly when her husband died unexpectedly. “When my healthy, long-distance runner husband died suddenly far from home three years ago, one of my first thoughts was of Don,” Jan said. “I needed that warm, pastoral hug that I associate so much with him. He is so compassionate and wise. Don will always be treasured”. Trustee Kara Baysinger, knowing Don’s love of baseball, regaled the audience by comparing Don’s many skills to team players, utility players (he can handle any role he’s asked to do), and pinch hitters. Emphasizing Don’s intellectual prowess, she added Yogi Berra’s famous quote, “Baseball is 90% mental, and the other half is physical.” Longtime church member Steven Thorne praised Don. “Don has been the spiritual and operational backbone for continuity and stability in this church,” Steven said. Church Trustee Steve Senter and Youth Pastor Scott Kail also showed their gratitude with personal observations. The final speaker, Senior Pastor Steve Schibsted, summarized Don’s excellence as a pastor. “To be a great pastor, you have to have both head and heart,” Steve said. “Don has both. He has a keen intellect. We have definitely experienced it in both his teaching and preaching. And, he has a big heart. He cares deeply Photos by Michael Barber Associate Pastor Don Ashburn, right, receives accolades from Senior Pastor Steve Schibsted during a celebration on Sunday, April 2, when he was honored for 20 years of service to Piedmont Community Church. Board of Trustees member Jan Wolfe and Don enjoy light banter Church member Steve Senter explains the many ways Don has helped him and his family over the years. With palm frond in hand, church member Joyce Hicks stands with husband Eric Behrens in the Courtyard. Nearly 100 people stayed after Sunday worship to acknowledge Don’s service to the church. about people. We have all experienced his love through his pastoral care. He has walked with many of us through some of our most difficult moments.” After these encomiums, Don shared what his 20 years of service and this celebration meant to him. “Twenty years has sure flown by,” he said. “My daughter, Maddy, was born the day I started working at the church and my son Griffin was only three. My family has sort of grown up in the Piedmont community. It’s been a great experience for us – especially now, with a real sense of revitalization at the church.” Days later, Don reflected on the gathering. “The celebration was great,” he said. “We managed to have a clear day, so it was nice to be outside with folks I’ve known and loved and served with for years.” Writer’s Note: Speaking from personal experience, my own family has been involved with Piedmont Community Church for as long as Don has, and he has been a very special part of our lives. The Piedmont Sports Hall of Fame inducted six former athletes on Saturday, April 8 at the new Alan Harvey Theater, marking the first time in recent years for the ceremony at a venue other than the Claremont Country Club. “This induction ceremony marks the 20th year of the Piedmont Sports Hall of Fame. It’s become an endearing tradition that recognizes, not only great teams and athletes, but coaches from Piedmont’s storied history as well… We’re very excited to start a new tradition here on the high school campus where those memories were made,” said Jim Stehr, the Piedmont Sports Hall of Fame host and a member of the first class of inductees. Inductees included Lauren Barbieri from the Class of 2001 (cross country, track), Devin Brown of the Class of 2009 (basketball, football), James Danielson from the Class of 1981 (football, soccer, track), Georgia Hill from the Class of 2013 (basketball, softball), Jon Minor from the Class of 1983 (basketball), and Kerri Roemer of the Class of 1999 (basketball, softball, tennis, track). Founded in 2003 by the late Ken Rawlings and Pete Anderson, and led for many years by former PHS and current Miramonte basketball coach Chris Lavdiotis, the Piedmont Sports Hall of Fame honors athletes, coaches, administrators, and community members for outstanding contributions to Piedmont High School athletics. Lavdiotis was honored prior to the start of the ceremony for his efforts to help create the Hall of Fame. He was planning only on a speech for the induction of Brown, a former player he coached. “This is a complete surprise… I had no idea this was happening, I came here to honor Devin Brown. He called Bebe Rawlings, because he was thinking about the same thing.’ And now it’s 20 years later. This is awesome,” said Lavdiotis. Piedmont’s boys’ tennis team wrapped up a highly productive week by sweeping three matches against league competition, defeating Alameda 7-0 on Tuesday April 4 on the road, beating Alameda again 6-1 on Wednesday, April 5 at home, and shutting out Arroyo 7-0 in San Lorenzo. The batch of wins brings Piedmont’s overall record to 10-4 and 7-1 against league opponents. The match to likely determine the fate of the Western Alameda County Conference title will be on April 26 when the Highlanders host league rivals, Berkeley. “We’re getting the job done against league competition. We have seven dual matches remaining for our regular season, and we know the big one is Berkeley,” said coach Jim Landes. 7-0 over Alameda Piedmont won all seven matches in straight sets against the Alameda Hornets. In singles, Lucas Smolko won at the No. 1 spot with a double-bagel win, 6-0, 6-0. At No. 2, Ben Breber also won 6-0, 6-0. At No. 3, Ethan Pham won 6-1, 6-0, while Alex Zalewski won at No. 4 in straight sets, 6-1, 6-1. In doubles, Monte Imburg and Nate Welch won 6-2, 6-1 at the No. 1 spot. articles.text: Piedmont High sent four athletes to compete in five events at the Arcadia Invitational on Friday and Saturday, April 7-8. The event is considered one of the most prestigious annual events for high school runners with some of the top athletes in the country making their way to the Arcadia HS track, marking the second-consecutive year for PHS be invited. “Parker Long, Christian Taylor, Xander Schulte-Sasse, and Sam Shelby qualified for and raced in arguably the most prestigious high school competition of the year. For reference, multiple U.S. Olympians have raced at the Arcadia Invitational while they were in high school. During the weekend, we saw one Parker Long (left) placed third of 52 at the prestigious Arcadia Invitational. all-time U.S. high school record fall, multiple top-10 all-time marks get hit, and a handful of Xander Schulte-Sasse (left), Parker Long, Christian Taylor, and Sam Shelby competed in the distance medley relay. No. 1 marks in the country for this season. “Simply put, this meet is the best of the best,” said Piedmont head coach Pouyan Assadi. It was a strong day for Parker Long, who placed third in a super fast 800-meters with a time of 1:53.35. He was .03 behind Caleb Levy from Gurnee, Illinois, and 1.17 seconds behind the winner, Colby Jenks of Big Piney, Wyoming. Assadi thinks Long was “boxed in” early on in his race, but the Piedmont runner was able to push through the crowded field. “Parker got boxed in but once an opening appeared, he took off and moved from ninth to seventh, and then finished third. He has incredible top-end speed. Once he adds a little aggressiveness to his race, he’ll take the next leap,” explained Assadi. “I knew I had a good chance to be one of the top finishers,” Long said after the race. “My plan was to go out near the front. I wanted to get a spot in Lane 1 until it was time to kick. There were guys in another section who went out a little faster than I did and they boxed me behind them. I came through the first lap in a not very good position. I wanted to wait for a straight section, and with 300 to go I made a big move. With 200 to go, I felt really confident because I saved up energy,” Long said. Parker was the top runner from the Northern California region in his event. He similarly ran to a third place finish at the Stanford Invitational on April 1 with a time of 1:53.77. “I got boxed into Lane 2 at Stanford and I didn’t like that. I knew it would be a big tactical match with positioning. I think my mistakes in both races came down to positioning on Lap 1. I’m still pretty new to the 800,” he said. Christian Taylor competed in three individual events and placed sixth of nine runners in each race: a time of 4:02.22 in the 1500 meters; 4:18.91 in the 1600; and 4:20.75 in the mile. Piedmont’s distance medley relay team of Xander Schulte-Sasse, Sam Shelby, Long, and Taylor, running distances of 1,200 meters, 400 meters, 800, meters and 1,600 meters respectively, placed 22nd of 26 teams. NEXT UP Piedmont returns from spring break on Thursday, April 20, and will host a league meet at Witter Field with Alameda, Bishop O’Dowd, Hayward, Mt. Eden, and Tennyson.

articles.text: The mountain bike team from Piedmont High raced at Fort Ord in Monterey during the Fun At the Fort races on Saturday, March 25, where racers competed on a 5.14 mile course. “It was a fantastic sunny day with the trails riding very well,” said coach Sally Aldridge. ”Fort Ord’s largely single track trails are in sandy terrain, so they drain quickly and are in good shape despite the huge amounts of rain we have experienced this winter. The Fort Ord race start is on a hill and is notorious for creating bottlenecks as riders jostle for position.” Jasper Schuetz won the Freshman Division 1 race with a twolap time of 40:42, clocking times of 20:28 and 20:13, impressively notching a faster time on his second lap. He currently leads the Interscholastic NorCal Cycling League’s D1 Freshman category after three races. Andres Robert placed 18th in the varsity boys’ race with a time of 1:01:47. Jasper Schuetz won the Freshman Div. 1 race at the Fun At the Fort event on Saturday, March 25. In the varsity boys’ category, Andres Robert placed 18th of 32 with a time of 1:01:47 in a threelap race, clocking times of 20:09, 21:17, and 20:20. Aleksi Valkonen placed 28th in 1:06:43. Junior Schuyler Sawicki placed seventh out of 74 riders in the JV boys’ Division 1 category, which puts him in fifth place overall this season after three races. Junior Mark Hsia also was 12th with a time of 43:20, and right behind were teammates Matteo Scanu (14th, 43:32) and Max Rivera (15th, 43:33). In the sophomore Div. 1 race, Cary Ward finished 12th of 42 racers in 46:33, and Ethan Becker was 36th in 1:00:09. Heather Stoneman finished 27th of 38 riders in the JV girls’ race, finishing with a time of 1:11:08 in the two-lap race. Anne Marie Gibbs was 34th in 1:19:07. Schuyler Sawicki placed seventh out of 74 riders in the junior varsity boys’ Division 1 category.

articles.text: Piedmont Swim Team, Piedmont’s independent year-round youth aquatics team, sent a record number of swimmers to compete in the Pacific Swimming Far Western Championships in late March. The 11 qualifiers were: Ryan Stokes (18), Simon Lins (18), Paige Arnold (17), Josie Oesterer (17), Sydney Olson (14), Evan Byun (15), Gabriel Reader (15), Nathan Judy (15), Asher Takazawa (14), Cole Carnazzo (14) and Connor Carnazzo (12). Far Westerns is a high level competition hosted by Pacific Swimming, the third largest region in USA Swimming. The meet, which took place over four days in Morgan Hill from March 30 to April 2, had 119 teams from throughout California, Nevada, Arizona, Oregon, and Utah with more than 1,100 swimmers. “To qualify, swimmers had to meet time standards ahead of time,” explained head coach Stefan Bill. “Those time standards are very fast and only a small percentage of swimmers in the USA get to that level.” The competition featured multiple national age group record holders and many senior high school swimmers that have been recruited to some of the top colCole Carnazzo (left), Head Coach Stefan Bill, Connor Carnazzo, Simon Lins & Paige Arnold leges in the country. “We had a fantastic meet,” said coach Bill. “Almost everyone made finals at least once.” Meet highlights included: • Team Captain Josie Oesterer achieved her first ever sectional cut. • Simon Lins won the 50 freestyle for ages 15-18. • Connor Carnazzo placed 2nd in the 100 backstroke (11-12 category). • Cole Carnazzo got his first sectional cut in the 200 fly and made multiple finals in the 13-14 category. • Asher Takazawa made finals in the 100 and 200 backstroke (13-14 category). • Gabe Reader, Evan Byun and Sydney Olson swam new personal best times. • Ryan Stokes, Paige Arnold and Nathan Judy had some amazing preliminary and finals swims. Though it was a long four days, coach Bill said, “To me as head coach, the most amazing thing was the positive attitude the swimmers and parents had during the meet –the cheerfulness, camaraderie and support the swimmers gave each other and the professionalism everyone displayed during the four days. Our athletes were just a pleasure to be around and to coach during this meet.” Paige Arnold (left), Josie Oesterer, Simon Lins, Connor Carnazzo, Cole Carnazzo, Asher Takazawa, Evan Byun, and Gabe Reader Josie Oesterer (left) and Paige Arnold.

articles.text: The Piedmont Junior Running Club, a Rec Department program for 4th and 5th graders, completed its winter season with a challenge race of one mile at Witter Field on March 8. Under sunny skies and with families looking on, 54 boys and girls from Piedmont elementary schools, in three different heats, ran four laps around the track (one mile) with the goal of trying to do better than their PR (personal record) time during the year for the “PE Mile.” Charley Harnett, a 5th grader Running coach Len Goldman is the founder of both the middle school cross-country program and the 4th and 5th grade Junior Running Club. Fourth and fifth grade members of the Piedmont Junior Running Club show their numbers at Witter Field. at Aurora School in Oakland won Heat 1 with a time of Seven minutes, 10 seconds (7:10). The winner of Heat 2 was Ben Centeno, a 4th grader at Wildwood, whose time was 6:48.3. In the final race of the day, Heat 3, Kenji Holt, a 5th grader at Wildwood, led from start to finish with a very good time of 6:06.4. The first girl overall was Henley Azad, a 5th grader at Havens, who comes from a high-achieving athletic family. Her mother, the former Courtney Gault, was a star basketball and softball player at Piedmont High School, and her uncle, Scott Gault, competed as a rower in two Olympic Games. Henley’s winning time was 6:26.8. Thanks to a grant from the Piedmont Turkey Trot, each runner wore a brand-new Piedmont Junior Running Club t-shirt at the event. The Winter session had one of the largest groups ever to participate in the program with a total of 62 students. What now? The Spring session began on March 27 and there may be some openings at Havens and Beach Schools. The Wildwood program is filled with 25 students registered. Registration is through the Piedmont Rec Department at 420-3070. For the first time, the Junior Running Club will offer a 4-week summer program, which will meet twice a week from July 10 to August 2 on Mondays and Wednesdays from 3:00 to 5:15 p.m. at Witter Field. Piedmont won 12 events on the afternoon. PHS’ 200 Free relay team of Lins, junior Tom Rolefson, and freshmen Dima Secor and Nik Costello won with a time of 1:32.78, picking up an NCS Consideration Time. He also won the 100 Back in 55.30, another NCS Consideration Time. Rolefson won the 50 Free in 23.19, while also finished third in 100 Free, 52.20. Sophomore Evan Byun won the 500 Free with a time of 5:29.23. He also won the 100 Breast with a time of 1:07.69. Nina Schwab wins in diving Piedmont High’s only diver, junior Nina Schwab, won the competition on March 30 at Berkeley High. In six dives, she scored 243 points, 50 better than the nearest competitor. NEXT UP The Piedmont High swim team will travel to Castro Valley on Thursday, April 13 for a 3:30 p.m. meet. Piedmont swimmers take on Far Westerns By Lisa Chan Carnazzo Piedmont Swim Team, Piedmont’s independent year-round youth aquatics team, sent a record number of swimmers to compete in the Pacific Swimming Far Western Championships in late March. The 11 qualifiers were: Ryan Stokes (18), Simon Lins (18), Paige Arnold (17), Josie Oesterer (17), Sydney Olson (14), Evan Byun (15), Gabriel Reader (15), Nathan Judy (15), Asher Takazawa (14), Cole Carnazzo (14) and Connor Carnazzo (12). Far Westerns is a high level competition hosted by Pacific Swimming, the third largest region in USA Swimming. The meet, which took place over four days in Morgan Hill from March 30 to April 2, had 119 teams from throughout California, Nevada, Arizona, Oregon, and Utah with more than 1,100 swimmers. “To qualify, swimmers had to meet time standards ahead of time,” explained head coach Stefan Bill. “Those time standards are very fast and only a small percentage of swimmers in the USA get to that level.” The competition featured multiple national age group record holders and many senior high school swimmers that have been recruited to some of the top colCole Carnazzo (left), Head Coach Stefan Bill, Connor Carnazzo, Simon Lins & Paige Arnold leges in the country. “We had a fantastic meet,” said coach Bill. “Almost everyone made finals at least once.” Meet highlights included: • Team Captain Josie Oesterer achieved her first ever sectional cut. • Simon Lins won the 50 freestyle for ages 15-18. • Connor Carnazzo placed 2nd in the 100 backstroke (11-12 category). • Cole Carnazzo got his first sectional cut in the 200 fly and made multiple finals in the 13-14 category. • Asher Takazawa made finals in the 100 and 200 backstroke (13-14 category). • Gabe Reader, Evan Byun and Sydney Olson swam new personal best times. • Ryan Stokes, Paige Arnold and Nathan Judy had some amazing preliminary and finals swims. Though it was a long four days, coach Bill said, “To me as head coach, the most amazing thing was the positive attitude the swimmers and parents had during the meet –the cheerfulness, camaraderie and support the swimmers gave each other and the professionalism everyone displayed during the four days. Our athletes were just a pleasure to be around and to coach during this meet.” Nina Schwab is the only diver at Piedmont High and won a recent competition at Berkeley High. Junior Running Club completes successful winter season By Steve Zirkelbach The Piedmont Junior Running Club, a Rec Department program for 4th and 5th graders, completed its winter season with a challenge race of one mile at Witter Field on March 8. Under sunny skies and with families looking on, 54 boys and girls from Piedmont elementary schools, in three different heats, ran four laps around the track (one mile) with the goal of trying to do better than their PR (personal record) time during the year for the “PE Mile.” Charley Harnett, a 5th grader Running coach Len Goldman is the founder of both the middle school cross-country program and the 4th and 5th grade Junior Running Club. Fourth and fifth grade members of the Piedmont Junior Running Club show their numbers at Witter Field. at Aurora School in Oakland won Heat 1 with a time of Seven minutes, 10 seconds (7:10). The winner of Heat 2 was Ben Centeno, a 4th grader at Wildwood, whose time was 6:48.3. In the final race of the day, Heat 3, Kenji Holt, a 5th grader at Wildwood, led from start to finish with a very good time of 6:06.4. The first girl overall was Henley Azad, a 5th grader at Havens, who comes from a high-achieving athletic family. Her mother, the former Courtney Gault, was a star basketball and softball player at Piedmont High School, and her uncle, Scott Gault, competed as a rower in two Olympic Games. Henley’s winning time was 6:26.8. Thanks to a grant from the Piedmont Turkey Trot, each runner wore a brand-new Piedmont Junior Running Club t-shirt at the event. The Winter session had one of the largest groups ever to participate in the program with a total of 62 students. What now? The Spring session began on March 27 and there may be some openings at Havens and Beach Schools. The Wildwood program is filled with 25 students registered. Registration is through the Piedmont Rec Department at 420-3070. For the first time, the Junior Running Club will offer a 4-week summer program, which will meet twice a week from July 10 to August 2 on Mondays and Wednesdays from 3:00 to 5:15 p.m. at Witter Field. articles.text: Treasure Island Museum welcomes organist Jerry Nagano for an afternoon concert on May 13. The lobby of the museum’s historic Building One will host the event, which showcases music that was popular during the 1950’s to 1970’s when the Treasure Island Naval Station was active. During that period, the Island’s Officers’ Club featured a family-friendly, Sunday dinner with organ music, often performed by local performer “Kay” Catherine Rooney. The organ which will be played by Nagano, a Los Angeles-based pianist, is the same Hammond organ that Rooney played. The organ has been donated to the Treasure Island Museum by Rooney’s niece, Chris Weicher, for the event. The concert begins at 2 p.m. For more information and to purchase tickets, visit https:// www.treasureislandmuseum. org/event-details/organ-concertwith-jerry-nagano-at-treasureisland-museum.

articles.text: The Diluvian Quartet will perform a Spring recital, Great Dedications, at the Piedmont Center for the Arts at 7 p.m. this Saturday, April 15. Elizabeth Castro Abrams and Jessica Scrimale, violins; Raphael Gold, viola; and Sylvia Woodmansee, cello will perform quartets by W.A. Mozart and Reinhold Gliere, celebrating two prolific composers and the works they dedicated to their most influential colleagues and teachers. Doors open at 6:45 p.m., and the concert begins at 7 p.m. A dessert reception and drinks will follow. Advance tickets are available at www.eventbrite.com/ e/582873007857. Tickets may also be purchased at the door. Highlights Mozart’s Quartet No. 15 is one of his greatest masterpieces. The second of a group of six quartets dedicated to the great Josef Haydn, his friend and mentor, it was the most profound quartet written at the time of its publication. It stands today as one of the most expressive works in the genre. It is marked by a dark and somber melody, at once giving way to a bright and cheerful theme over and over, always with Mozart’s genius ability at musical conversation. Born in Kiev, Ukraine, Reinhold Glière went on to be one of the most important Soviet composers of his generation. The piece on this program, his 2nd quartet, was written in 1905, and was dedicated to the great Russian composer Nikolai Rimsky-Korsakov. It is jampacked with themes of Imperial Czarist Russia, lush romantic chords, unabashed emotional expression, and toe-tapping rhythmic gestures. This program features some of the most beautiful music ever written for string quartets. The Diluvian Quartet has been playing together for two years and prides itself on diverse programs that combine standards of the repertoire with lesser-known masterpieces.

articles.text: San Francisco Museum of Modern Art (SF MOMA) is now showing the works of sculptor Alexander Calder, famous for his intricate mobiles. The exhibit, Dissonant Harmony, will be on view through May. Calder was an American sculpture best known for his whimsical, colorful and geometric mobiles. His first solo exhibition in 1926 at the Gallery of Jacques Seligmann in Paris brought critical success. He later exhibited in top art galleries and museums around the world. His work is now included in permanent collections at the Museum of Modern Art and the Guggenheim in New York, as well as the Centre Georges Pompidou in Paris. The Whitney Museum in New York City currently holds the largest permanent collection of Calder’s sculptures. Visit San Francisco Museum of Modern Art to see well-known Calder pieces like Lone Yellow (1961), Maquette for The Cello Player (1958), and Double Gong (1953). To learn more, and to purchase tickets to SF MOMA, visit https:// www.sfmoma.org/exhibition/ alexander-calder-dissonant-harmony/. Sculptor and mobile creator Alexander Calder.
articles.title: Alexander Calder exhibit at SF MOMA through May

articles.text: San Francisco’s Museum of the African Diaspora (MoAD) celebrates Black beauty and femininity with its current exhibit, Black Venus, on view now through August 20. The exhibition is curated by Aindrea Emelife and is a reflection of the legacy of Black Women in visual culture, from colonial-era caricatures to the reclamation of Black womanhood by 18 artists of numerous nationalities and ages. Artwork spans from 1793 to the present day. Featured artists include Alberta Whittle, Amber Pinkerton, Ayana V. Jackson, Carrie Mae Weems, Carla Williams, Coreen Simpson, Deana Lawson, Deborah Roberts, Frida Orupabo, Ming Smith, Kara Walker, Maud Sulter, Lorna Simpson, Renee Cox, Sadie Barnette, Shawanda Corbett, Tabita Rezaire, Taiye Idahor, Wangechi Mutu, Yetunde Olagbaju and Zanele Muholi. The exhibition’s thematic foundation is the Hottentot Venus, a visual-culture archetype named for the assigned stage name of Saartje Baartman (born 1789 in South Africa. To learn more and to purchase tickets to the museum, visit https://www.moadsf.org/exhibitions/black-venus. The exhibition’s thematic foundation is the Hottentot Venus.

articles.text: Asian Art Museum in San Francisco is currently exhibiting Beyond Bollywood: 2000 Years of Dance in Art beginning March 31. The new exhibition features more than 120 artworks borrowed from 20 of the finest museums and private collections in the world, with a focus on the arts of the Indian cultural sphere. Beyond Bollywood includes artwork from India, Pakistan, Nepal, Tibet, Sri Lanka, Myanmar, Thailand, Cambodia, and Indonesia. “We hope visitors will come away with a transformed notion of the importance and power of dance,” said exhibition co-curator Forrest McGill. “[Both] what it has meant in the past, and what it can mean in their own lives today.” Burmese artifact c. 1857; wood with lacquer, gold leaf and inlaid glass Beyond Bollywood will be on display through July 10. For more information, and to purchase tickets to the museum, visit https://exhibitions.asianart. org/exhibitions/beyond-bollywood-2000-years-of-dance-inart/.

articles.text: The Rider, written and directed by Academy Award-winning director Chloé Zhao, is a beautifully made film, so close to its stoic truth that it easily qualifies as cinema verité. The actors essentially played themselves with a naturalness that astonishes. The film is also a Western, wrapped in certain familiar tropes while at the same time being devoid of anything not realistic, which so often defines the Hollywood stories of the early west. The Rider is set on the Pine Ridge Reservation in South Dakota where director Chloé Zhao met Brady Jandreau, who is at the center of the film. He essentially plays himself; his character’s name is Brady Blackburn. His father, in the film, Tim Blackburn, is played by his real father, Tim Jandreau. Brady’s sister, Lilly Blackburn, is his actual sister, Lilly Jandreau, who is on the autism spectrum. His friends are his friends. All are untrained actors, yet they possess an unexpected verisimilitude that lends a remarkable authenticity to the narrative. The film opens with Brady dreaming of horses. Waking, he walks into the bathroom where we see a bandage covering the right side of his head. Slowly he removes the bandage, revealing a stapled half-moon scar. It is ugly in its seriousness, a foreshadowing of what lies ahead for Brady. In bits and pieces, we learn that the injury is from being stepped on by a rodeo bronco after being bucked off, resulting in a plate being inserted just beneath the wound. The implications for Brady are life changing, and he is confronted painfully with the reality that he likely will never be able to do what he deeply loves: rodeoing, riding horses, and training semi-wild horses. It is a gift which is his seemingly magical ability to communicate with these large animals. This is a gorgeously shot film, steeped in an expansive geography, creating a prose-like, metaphorical backdrop for a people who live on the far margins of the American dream. The double-wide mobile homes are surrounded by a landscape of tallgrass prairie, as silent and spare as the people who inhabit it. It’s a place where Brady is completely at home, but also caught in his self-imposed distance that speaks volumes as the camera holds on his sharply constructed young face (he’s 22). The Rider inhabits a middle ground between fiction and real life, and yet it avoids even a moment of gratuitous drama. It is harsh yet sensitive, beautiful and gritty as Brady resists and struggles with the truth of a life he had never planned for. The Rider. Directed by Chloé Zhao. Starring Brady Jandreau, Tim Jandreau, Scott Lane. 1 hr., 44 min. Rated R. Released in 2018. Now streaming on Prime/ Hulu/Vudu/Apple tv. Brady Jandreau in The Rider
articles.title: The Rider a beautiful film by Chloé Zhao

articles.text: Know first that Embrace of the Serpent was nominated for an Oscar for Best Foreign Language film from Colombia. Written and directed by David Gallego and photographed in black and white by Gallego, it is set in the heart of Colombia’s Amazon rainforest. Its images are luminous, the scale of its expansive beauty breathtaking. As well, it possesses a depth of melancholy that is unrelenting, for above all it is an allegory as well as a tribute to the indigenous people of the Amazon whose voices are now silent and whose cultures have vanished. The film opens in 1909 as a German ethnographer, Theo (based on the diaries of real life explorer Theodor Koch-Grunberg), portrayed by Jan Bijovet, is deathly ill. He convinces a young shaman, Karamakate (Nibio Torres), to take him up river in search of a plant, the yakruna, which is thought to have healing properties. Karamakate is initially reluctant; he rages at the rubber barons who have decimated his tribe and the ecosystem of the forest. Theo convinces him that if he will act as their guide he will show him where his people, called the Cohiuano, are, insisting they still exist. Karamakate reluctantly agrees. And so, along with Theo’s river Sherpa, the three men begin their journey in a dugout canoe in search of the sacred plant. It is a trip that takes them into Joseph Conrad’s Heart of Darkness. One of the most unsettling moments of the film occurs at a mission where a priest has taken in a group of orphan boys, their parents killed in the rubber wars. Theo finds that the priest is physically abusive and regards his charges as pagans and beats them remorselessly. Running parallel to the story of Theo is that of Evan (Brionne Davis), a character based on the American botanist, Richard Evans Schultes, who, using Theo’s diary and sketches, is also in search of the elusive plant, and its medicinal properties. Forty years later, the guide is once again a now aged Karamakate who agrees to take Evan (as he’s called). Like Theo, they stop at the decaying mission, only now it’s inhabited by a cult that worships a madman who believes he is Jesus. Embedded in the film is one overriding question: what does it mean to be civilized? Can those who called the indigenous people “savages” or “pagans” the carriers of truth? Can they call themselves civilized? What followed in their wake amounted to the genocide of groups of people, decimated by disease and forced labor for the profit of the rubber barons who were unconscionably rapacious. But know that the film is not heavy-handed or overbearing. There is instead an inherent sadness to the story; it is elegiac in its composition, the images startling, evocative, and often unexpected. It is unlike any film you will have seen before. Do not expect a story that relies on lengthy exposition; there is no coherent narrative arc. It is as much a visual experience with almost a documentary feel that borders on the mythical and the surreal, framed by the emotions of grief and loss. Embrace of the Serpent. Directed by Ciro Guerra. In Spanish with subtitles. Starring Jan Bijvoet, Brionne Davis, Nilbio Torres. 2 hrs., 3 min, Not rated. Released in 2016. Nominated for Academy Award for Best Foreign feature length film.
articles.title: Embrace of the Serpent a look at the loss of indigenous cultures in the Amazon

He essentially plays himself; his character’s name is Brady Blackburn. His father, in the film, Tim Blackburn, is played by his real father, Tim Jandreau. Brady’s sister, Lilly Blackburn, is his actual sister, Lilly Jandreau, who is on the autism spectrum. His friends are his friends. All are untrained actors, yet they possess an unexpected verisimilitude that lends a remarkable authenticity to the narrative. The film opens with Brady dreaming of horses. Waking, he walks into the bathroom where we see a bandage covering the right side of his head. Slowly he removes the bandage, revealing a stapled half-moon scar. It is ugly in its seriousness, a foreshadowing of what lies ahead for Brady. In bits and pieces, we learn that the injury is from being stepped on by a rodeo bronco after being bucked off, resulting in a plate being inserted just beneath the wound. The implications for Brady are life changing, and he is confronted painfully with the reality that he likely will never be able to do what he deeply loves: rodeoing, riding horses, and training semi-wild horses. It is a gift which is his seemingly magical ability to communicate with these large animals. This is a gorgeously shot film, steeped in an expansive geography, creating a prose-like, metaphorical backdrop for a people who live on the far margins of the American dream. The double-wide mobile homes are surrounded by a landscape of tallgrass prairie, as silent and spare as the people who inhabit it. It’s a place where Brady is completely at home, but also caught in his self-imposed distance that speaks volumes as the camera holds on his sharply constructed young face (he’s 22). The Rider inhabits a middle ground between fiction and real life, and yet it avoids even a moment of gratuitous drama. It is harsh yet sensitive, beautiful and gritty as Brady resists and struggles with the truth of a life he had never planned for. The Rider. Directed by Chloé Zhao. A scene from Embrace of the Serpent Embrace of the Serpent a look at the loss of indigenous cultures in the Amazon By Chris Honore’ Know first that Embrace of the Serpent was nominated for an Oscar for Best Foreign Language film from Colombia. Written and directed by David Gallego and photographed in black and white by Gallego, it is set in the heart of Colombia’s Amazon rainforest. Its images are luminous, the scale of its expansive beauty breathtaking. As well, it possesses a depth of melancholy that is unrelenting, for above all it is an allegory as well as a tribute to the indigenous people of the Amazon whose voices are now silent and whose cultures have vanished. The film opens in 1909 as a German ethnographer, Theo (based on the diaries of real life explorer Theodor Koch-Grunberg), portrayed by Jan Bijovet, is deathly ill. He convinces a young shaman, Karamakate (Nibio Torres), to take him up river in search of a plant, the yakruna, which is thought to have healing properties. Karamakate is initially reluctant; he rages at the rubber barons who have decimated his tribe and the ecosystem of the forest. Theo convinces him that if he will act as their guide he will show him where his people, called the Cohiuano, are, insisting they still exist. Karamakate reluctantly agrees. And so, along with Theo’s river Sherpa, the three men begin their journey in a dugout canoe in search of the sacred plant. It is a trip that takes them into Joseph Conrad’s Heart of Darkness. One of the most unsettling moments of the film occurs at a mission where a priest has taken in a group of orphan boys, their parents killed in the rubber wars. Theo finds that the priest is physically abusive and regards his charges as pagans and beats them remorselessly. Running parallel to the story of Theo is that of Evan (Brionne Davis), a character based on the American botanist, Richard Evans Schultes, who, using Theo’s diary and sketches, is also in search of the elusive plant, and its medicinal properties. Forty years later, the guide is once again a now aged Karamakate who agrees to take Evan (as he’s called). Like Theo, they stop at the decaying mission, only now it’s inhabited by a cult that worships a madman who believes he is Jesus. Embedded in the film is one overriding question: what does it mean to be civilized? Can those who called the indigenous people “savages” or “pagans” the carriers of truth? Can they call themselves civilized? What followed in their wake amounted to the genocide of groups of people, decimated by disease and forced labor for the profit of the rubber barons who were unconscionably rapacious. But know that the film is not heavy-handed or overbearing. There is instead an inherent sadness to the story; it is elegiac in its composition, the images startling, evocative, and often unexpected. It is unlike any film you will have seen before. Do not expect a story that relies on lengthy exposition; there is no coherent narrative arc. It is as much a visual experience with almost a documentary feel that borders on the mythical and the surreal, framed by the emotions of grief and loss. Embrace of the Serpent. Hence, it wasn’t long before Pinocchio became an iconic figure, and audiences soon regarded the fairy tale about a small wooden puppet that was turned into a real boy as a classic The story opens with Jiminy Cricket (Cliff Edwards) explaining how an elderly Italian woodcarver, Geppetto (Christian Rub), creates a small wooden puppet. The old man, who lives alone, is so taken with the marionette, who he calls Pinocchio, before falling asleep, he gazes into the night sky and wishes upon a star that his wooden creation be turned into a real boy. This is Disney and so that night the puppet is visited by the Blue Fairy (Evelyn Venable) who promises to grant Geppetto his wish; however, there are conditions. If Pinocchio truly wants to be fully human, he must be brave, truthful and unselfish. And so begins the puppet’s journey, filled with moments that test his character. Will he tell the truth? Will he risk everything inside a monstrous whale and rescue Geppetto? Will he resist the temptations of some unsavory characters such as a con artist fox named Honest John (Walter Catlett). It is at such moments that Jiminy Cricket steps forward and takes on the role of Pinocchio’s conscience and guide, reminding him of his promise to the Blue Fairy. The guild of animators who faithfully brought Collodi’s story to the screen were artists in the truest sense of the word, and that is why this beautiful film will never lose its compelling magic. articles.text: At age six, Wynton Marsalis was seated at a table with the great trumpeters Al Hirt, Miles Davis and Clark Terry. His father, a pianist, joked that he should get Wynton a trumpet, too. Al Hirt gave him one. When eight, he played with the Fairview Baptist Church band led by legendary banjoist Danny Barker, and at 14 was with the New Orleans Philharmonic. During high school, he performed with the New Orleans Symphony Brass Quintet, New Orleans Community Concert Band, New Orleans Youth Orchestra, New Orleans Symphony, local jazz bands and the funk band The Creators. Wynton began classical training at 12, and at 17 was studying at Julliard Conservatory in New York and playing with The Jazz Messengers and Art Blakey. Wynton and his saxophonist brother Branford are credited with championing overlooked jazz musicians, prompting a jazz renaissance in the early 1980’s. His band performed over 120 Trumpeter Wynton Marsalis concerts each year from 1981 to 1996. Wynton has performed with a diversity of artists and styles. In jazz, he’s performed with Sarah Vaughan, Dizzy Gillespie, Clark Terry, John Lewis, Sonny Rollins, Christian McBride, Ron Carter, Herbie Hancock and Tony Williams. In classical music, he has appeared with the New York Philharmonic, Los Angeles Philharmonic, Boston Pops, Cleveland Orchestra, English Chamber Orchestra, London Royal Philharmonic and many others. In 2008, Wynton recorded Two Men with the Blues with Willie Nelson. In the 2019 Ken Burns documentary Country Music, Wynton explored the shared roots found through American music. In 2011, Eric Clapton and Wynton performed Play the Blues: Live from Jazz at Lincoln Center and released it on an album. Wynton was the first to be awarded a Grammy for jazz and classical in the same year (1983) and has received a total of nine Grammy awards. He has recorded many classical albums and performed with notable orchestras around the world. In 1987, he founded the Jazz At Lincoln Center series. A crowning achievement was winning the Pulitzer Prize for Music in 1997. Always swinging, Wynton plays with a clear tone, depth of emotion and a rich tonal palette of melodic and trumpet techniques, including vocal effects (slides, growls, smears, halfvalve effects, tremolo, shakes, plunger), rhythmic displacement and tension resolution (melodic, harmonic and rhythmic). I could tell that the woman in the kitchen Good home cookin’ – was the owner. She was friendly and efficient. Ethiopian style I looked into the small kitchen and saw that everything was made to order. This was a very good sign. Another was that all of the customers were Ethiopian. My wife ordered a sandwich and I got the vegetarian stew. In a few minutes, the owner brought our food. The portions were huge. My traditional Ethiopian stew was made of fava beans, tomatoes, onion, and Eritrean spices. It was served with two large French rolls, which were just about the best I’ve had outside of France. The crust was light and flaky, and the inside light and tender. Alems has a diverse menu, which includes American style sandwiches, and traditional Ethiopian/Eritrean cuisine. While you are enjoying the food there you will enjoy chatting with the customers and the owner…if she has a moment to chat. For homework, read the history of Ethiopia/Eritrea. for musical inspiration listen to Verdi‘s opera Aida. If you are interested in military history, you will be interested to know that the Ethiopians used animals as their allies. By using bees, wasps, lions and elephants, they were invaded but never conquered. articles.text: Walking through town it is impossible not to notice the aesthetic impact of different ancillary structures that are an integral part of the design of many homes. Falling somewhere between architecture and landscape architecture, fences, walls, and their associated gates are chief among these. They can enhance (or unfortunately sometimes compromise) the building, landscape and/or site design. So…what constitutes nice retaining walls, appealing fences or beautiful gates? Like all of the discussions in this column, I point out different ideas or considerations that hopefully help to answer this ongoing question. But there are usually many good answers as well as exceptions to every general rule. What is ultimately important is just what looks and feels right – what appeals to us. That being said, here are some thoughts. The first thing that comes to mind is that these secondary structures need as much study and consideration as the main building(s) or landscape treatment of which they are a part. It is unfortunately obvious when they are designed as simply an afterthought. Fences, walls and gates certainly must be in the same architectural “family” as the home, though this doesn’t mean they have to be exactly the same form, color or even the same material. They do need to relate most appropriately. They are indeed an opportunity to aesthetically deviate to some degree and add interest to both the building(s) and property. Fences or walls can be used to provide privacy, add security, or merely to demarcate the edge of private or semi-private spaces between adjacent properties, or between a property and the street. Photos and sketch by Will Adams Photos above and below: Two well designed variations of the traditional white picket fence, both stepping to nicely accommodate the slope of the sidewalk and site, as well as adding interest and texture to the street. After adherence to the architectural style of the buildings, the intended use or function of the barrier will be the primary consideration in determining its type, shape and character, i.e., solid (wall) vs, airy (spaced boards), height, extent, and access or gate placements. Gates are, of course, a prominent part of fences and walls, almost automatically seen as a punctuation point because they usually break the horizontal character of the enclosure to which they are attached. Gates are the first thing people use and pass-through in the “entry experience”, as we mentioned in a Photos above: Two elegantly designed gates of completely different architectural styles. Both are perfectly suited to the walled enclosures of which they are a part and enhance and complement their associated building architecture.

pages.text: Wednesday, Aprl 12, 2023 23 The Wine Corner The Wines of the Northern Rhone By Pierre DuMont After a two-year hiatus because of the COVID pandemic. I was able to resume my annual European wine trip with my colleagues Richard Wing and Terry Hershey. This year we decided to head to the Northern Rhone Valley in Southern France, the original home to two of the greatest grape varietals on earth, Syrah and Viognier. We split our time between the northern part of the area centered on Cote Rotie and Condrieu, and the southern part of Hermitage, St. Joseph and Cornas (to be reviewed in the next article.) Cote Rotie The main wine growing area of the Rhone Valley begins about 10 miles south of the ancient Roman city of Vienne. The northernmost appellation is Cote Rotie (the Roasted Slope). It is a high, slanted hillside that is tilted to face the sun and gather the most warmth. The slope is one of the steepest places in the world where wine is grown, making the growing of these grapes incredibly arduous and time consuming. Most places are far too steep for machinery to be used, so everything must be done by hand or by horse. The only red grape allowed in the Northern Rhone is Syrah, and in Cote Rotie it is allowed to mix in some Viognier which can add some interesting floral notes to the wine. The wines of Cote Rotie have been described as “an iron fist in a velvet glove.” They are full and powerful but also elegant and stylish. Pierre Gaillard Our first visit in Cote Rotie was with Pierre Gaillard and his family. Both of his daughters are winemakers with their own brands. Gaillard is based in the ancient town of Malleval founded in the 11th century and still looking like it. Just making your way through the narrow, winding streets is a challenge, to say nothing of when a car comes from the other direction. The Gaillard winery is modern and perched on the edge of town. Pierre was originally from Lyon and did not grow up in the wine business, He decided to make it his life after moving to Francois Villard Christine Vernay, master of Condrieu Lunch with the Gaillard family this area about 40 years ago. He now owns land in Cote Rotie, St. Joseph, Crozes Hermitage and Condrieu. Most of the current vintage of his wines were sold out – a good problem to have. We spent the morning barrel tasting the wines that will be bottled soon. The 2021 vintage was a difficult one in the Rhone; cold and wet weather, even hail, made it tough to mature the grapes. It is hard to complain though, as the Rhone has had a string of great vintages going back to 2014. The tasting by the Gaillard family was incredibly generous, and we ended up trying 23 different wines from the three family properties. If the only Syrahs and Viogniers you have had are from California, you are in for a change of pace. The climate of the Northern Rhone is much colder than California. That results in the wines having more acid and structure. When Viognier is grown in a warm climate it often becomes dull and f labby and Syrah becomes too fruity and sweet. The Rhone versions have incredible balance between fruit and acid and have an earthiness and minerality you don’t find elsewhere. What followed the tasting was one of the highlights of the entire trip. Pierre invited us to join his wife Pascale and daughter Jeanne for lunch at his house. Pascale whipped up an amazing meal of shaved truffles and mushrooms, roast pork and some vegetable I had never seen that was delicious. Pierre dove deep in the cellar and we drank Cote Rotie going back to 2000 finishing with a beautiful Banyuls dessert wine from his estate. We had two more tastings scheduled for the afternoon, but thankfully they were small and uneventful unlike the gargantuan culinary and wine experience at Gaillard. Francois Villard Francois Villard is one of the up-and-coming bright lights in the Rhone Valley. After previous careers as a chef and sommelier, he ventured into wine growing in 1991 with a small parcel of vines in Condrieu which he has expanded into holdings in Cote Rotie. Villard’s style has evolved from the big, heavy oak-laden style of wines that were popular in the 90’s (and still are with Guigal) to more elegant finesse-style wines attained by short fermentations with mostly full clusters. The wines have tremendous perfume and are exquisitely balanced and refreshing. I also appreciate that in a world where wine prices have gotten absolutely crazy, Villard has held the line and his wines represent great values. We tasted 20 wines at Villard and the highlights were the four Condrieu he produces. Each was intense and floral with a huge bouquet of peaches and melon with notes of honeysuckle and a big round mouthfeel but with balance and a stylish, non-cloying finish. He also makes an outstanding Cornas called Jouvet that is a monster wine with huge blackberry fruit and enough tannin and structure to last three decades. After the tasting Francois took us to a restaurant in the center of Ampuis called Bistro de Serrines. Francois is one of the owners, so we had no problem getting a table. The food was delicious, and this unassuming place had a wine list of over 700 wines including many of the most famous names of the Rhone Valley. Highly recommended if you are ever in the area. Georges Vernay Vernay is the most legendary name in Condrieu with an amazing backstory. The Condrieu appellation is the home of the Viognier grape and originally the only place in the world where it was planted. During the 1950’s and 60’s production it had declined to the point when there were only a few hectares left of the grape varietal in the world. George Vernay saw that the disappearance of Viognier would be a tragedy and began to convince other farmers to replant the varietal and even increase acres under vines. The magnificence of the wines began to be rediscovered and Condrieu appellation once more gained its stature as a gem of the Rhone Valley. Viognier vines were exported from Condrieu and planted in California, Australia, Chile, Argentina and many other locations, and is now a popular international varietal that is alive and well – thanks to George Vernay. This flagship estate is now run by daughter Christine Vernay and her husband Paul. Walking through the doors I felt I was entering the holy grail of Viognier. Christine herself poured the wines and talked about the minimalist methods she uses to make them. The flagship is called the Coteau du Vernon from the best located vineyard on the steep Condrieu slope. Equally good I thought was the Les Chaillees de L’Enfer (Steps of Hell) from a place on the hill that gets extremely hot hence the name. Both wines exude honeysuckle and gardenia aromas with luscious peach and apricot fruit with just the right amount of acid for balance. They were full and mouth-filling yet refreshing. To start your tasting journey into the Northern Rhone, the wines listed below are recommended as a beginning. The wines of Pierre Gaillard and Francois Villard are imported by Napa-based Jack Edwards Collection (jackedwardscollection. com) an outstanding source for European boutique wineries. articles.text: World War II ended too soon for Terry Rollin Haws to earn his Army Air Corp wings. So when, on March 19, 2023, he donned his well-deserved and glorious Angelic Wings, he was able to fly upward and onward to his next great adventure. Born in Piedmont on February 24, 1926, he was the only child of Magnolia Cosgrove Haws and Alpheus Haws and lived to be 97. He graduated from Piedmont High School in 1943, and earned a Bachelor’s degree from the University of California in Berkeley, where he was a track star. Some of Terry’s favorite childhood memories were the times he spent at Russian River with his family. He always looked back on his college years fondly. In his senior year at Berkeley, he began dating and subsequently married the love of his life for 71 years, Jacqueline Nino Haws. Terry began working full time for Haws Drinking Faucet Company in Berkeley in 1949, devoting his knowledge and expertise to the family company that was started in 1906 by his grandfather, Luther Ensign Haws, after he invented and patented the first drinking fountain. Under Terry’s leadership, Haws Drinking Faucet Company grew from a small local company into an internationally renowned manufacturer of drinking fountains and emergency equipment with locations in Switzerland, Singapore and Brazil. Terry and Jackie’s first child was a son, Timothy John Haws, whose short life prompted them to keep trying. Their first daughter, Nina Dori Haws, arrived in 1955. Her subsequent Downs Syndrome diagnosis introduced Terry and Jackie to a life of charitable community work. They committed themselves to a lifetime of supporting, developing and funding Las Trampas School for the developmentally disabled. Terry’s leadership on the Las Trampas Board of Directors for over 50 years allowed the organization to flourish and adapt to the changing needs of their clients and the community. In addition to his commitment to his business and philanthropy, Terry was also a devoted and loving father to his three daughters, Nina, Amy and Sallie. He provided and supported endless opportunities for them to participate in swimming, waterskiing, tennis, golf, dance, and music. Terry loved boating on the Delta. A member of Little Venice Yacht Club for over 30 years, he and Jackie made fabulous lasting memories with other members Born and raised in Piedmont, Terry Haws passed away in Lafayette on March 29 at age 97. who became lifelong friends. For almost 20 years after Little Venice closed, Terry and Jackie would spend as much time as they could on their houseboat at Bethel Harbor enjoying a libation on the back deck. After discovering the Big Island of Hawaii when he was nine years old, the Kohala Coast became one of Terry and Jackie’s favorite destination vacations as adults. For five decades they returned year after year to Mauna Kea and Kona Village Resort, and then enjoyed a family home in Kailua-Kona until 2019. A long-time member of the Orinda Country Club, Terry enjoyed golfing into his early nineties. Watching football and reading novels were two of his favorite pastimes he enjoyed until his very last days. Terry’s love, generosity, kindness and wonderful sense of humor created a legacy that will last forever. He was an exceptional father, husband, friend and businessman, who was greatly loved and admired by so many whose lives he touched. Terry Haws is survived by his beloved wife, Jacqueline, his two daughters and sons-in-law, Amy and Dennis Peck of Escondido, California and Sallie Haws and Jim Bowers of Henderson, Nevada; and his two grandchildren, Marquise and Terry Van Tassel of Henderson, Nevada. A memorial and Celebration of Life was held on Saturday, April 8, 2023. In lieu of flowers, the family requests memorial contributions be made to Las Trampas, P.O. Box 515, Lafayette, CA 94549. lastrampas.org/waysto-donate, or a restricted donation to the Bruns House Hospice East Bay, 3470 Buskirk Ave., Pleasant Hill, CA 94523. hospiceeastbay. org/campaign-for-bruns.

articles.text: The Walking on Wednesdays group got some lovely, spring weather last Wednesday. As some passed the top of Piedmont Park, they were taken back by the beauty of cherry trees in full blossom. An excellent turnout of 32 walkers were at the Exedra for a fun, special walk. The walkers had heard about pickleball, so Helen and Quincy Dong were asked to take the Wednesday Walkers to Linda/ Beach to see pickleball in action. Helen took the group down Magnolia Avenue past the high school. Work on the new aquatics center was fully underway. A very large Deere backhoe was scooping large amounts of earth out of a very large hole where the old pool once was and dumping them into a very large truck with another one waiting. Helen stopped in front of the middle school and told the walkers about the pickleball courts behind the school. The large group continued down Oakland and regrouped for a mass crossing of Grand Avenue, and up to the playfield next to Beach School. The walkers above the field on Howard Avenue made their way down and around the turf playfield that was being used by young Beach students in a P.E. class. The group came out on Linda Avenue and went up to the court entrance. The walkers went behind three sets of four pickleballers to an open area where they could watch the action. Lucy Chiang thoughtfully provided some rackets and encouraged the walkers to try the game. Pickleballer Rick Schiller came over and talked about the benefits of the sport. It was fun, but soon time for the walkers to make their way back up Oakland Avenue. The Dongs stayed to play, so the leader baton was handed off by Helen to Jim Kellogg for the return to the Exedra. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 a.m. Everyone is invited to join the group and there is no charge. Registration with the Piedmont Recreation Department is required at https://tinyurl. com/3ethkehu. Terry and Jackie’s first child was a son, Timothy John Haws, whose short life prompted them to keep trying. Their first daughter, Nina Dori Haws, arrived in 1955. Her subsequent Downs Syndrome diagnosis introduced Terry and Jackie to a life of charitable community work. They committed themselves to a lifetime of supporting, developing and funding Las Trampas School for the developmentally disabled. Terry’s leadership on the Las Trampas Board of Directors for over 50 years allowed the organization to flourish and adapt to the changing needs of their clients and the community. In addition to his commitment to his business and philanthropy, Terry was also a devoted and loving father to his three daughters, Nina, Amy and Sallie. He provided and supported endless opportunities for them to participate in swimming, waterskiing, tennis, golf, dance, and music. Terry loved boating on the Delta. A member of Little Venice Yacht Club for over 30 years, he and Jackie made fabulous lasting memories with other members Born and raised in Piedmont, Terry Haws passed away in Lafayette on March 29 at age 97. who became lifelong friends. For almost 20 years after Little Venice closed, Terry and Jackie would spend as much time as they could on their houseboat at Bethel Harbor enjoying a libation on the back deck. After discovering the Big Island of Hawaii when he was nine years old, the Kohala Coast became one of Terry and Jackie’s favorite destination vacations as adults. For five decades they returned year after year to Mauna Kea and Kona Village Resort, and then enjoyed a family home in Kailua-Kona until 2019. A long-time member of the Orinda Country Club, Terry enjoyed golfing into his early nineties. Watching football and reading novels were two of his favorite pastimes he enjoyed until his very last days. Terry’s love, generosity, kindness and wonderful sense of humor created a legacy that will last forever. He was an exceptional father, husband, friend and businessman, who was greatly loved and admired by so many whose lives he touched. Terry Haws is survived by his beloved wife, Jacqueline, his two daughters and sons-in-law, Amy and Dennis Peck of Escondido, California and Sallie Haws and Jim Bowers of Henderson, Nevada; and his two grandchildren, Marquise and Terry Van Tassel of Henderson, Nevada.
